warmup.q: A loop runs Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); sum += p.x() + p.y(); a million times, and p is never stored anywhere. Once the loop's method is hot and compiled by C2, how many bytes does one call allocate?
options: It depends on the heap size
warmup.why: C2's escape analysis sees that p never leaves the method, so it keeps x and y in registers and never creates the object. In one run the first rounds allocated megabytes while the code ran in the interpreter and C1, and later rounds allocated 0. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes. The heap size plays no part.

sections.h: Allocating an object is a pointer bump
sections.html:
Allocation on the JVM is cheap, and the reason is the TLAB, the thread-local allocation buffer.

New objects go into eden, the area of the heap where every object starts its life (lesson 4 covers the rest of the heap). Every thread shares eden, so if each new took memory from it directly, all threads would fight over one pointer. Instead, each thread claims a chunk of eden for itself and allocates inside it with no locking at all. In a JDK 21 trace of a small test JVM, each chunk was about 266 KB.

Allocating inside a TLAB means bumping a "top" pointer. This is HotSpot's fast path, from the JDK 25 source:

HeapWord* obj = top();
if (pointer_delta(end(), obj) >= size) {   // does the object fit?
  set_top(obj + size);                     // bump the pointer
  return obj;
}
return nullptr;                            // no: take the slow path

A compare, an add and a store. Then the JVM writes the header and zeroes the fields. In compiled code, the JIT inlines all of this into your method.

The slow path runs when the object doesn't fit. Usually the TLAB is simply full, and the thread takes a fresh one from eden with one atomic update. Objects too big for a TLAB go straight into eden. G1, the default garbage collector, splits the heap into equal regions of 1 to 32 MB, and an object bigger than half a region is humongous: a 3 MB byte[] on a heap with 2 MB regions skips TLABs and eden entirely. Lesson 4 shows why that costs more.

So the new itself is cheap. What you pay for is the rate. Every TLAB brings the next young collection closer: the GC run that empties eden once it's full. A service that allocates 1 GB a second fills a 500 MB eden twice a second, and with G1 every full eden means a young collection pause. The objects that are already dead cost almost nothing at that point, because a young collection copies only the survivors. Kotlin compiles to the same new bytecode, so all of this is identical in both languages.

try.title: Count TLAB refills
steps: Read TlabDemo. It allocates 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes, 80 MB in all, in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. Predict: how many times will the main thread go back to eden for a fresh TLAB?
Run it with the command below.
Find GC(1) TLAB totals. Divide the bytes the pause freed by refills.

code.title: TlabDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 2,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ public class TlabDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), TlabDemo.class.getName(), "allocate")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) sink = new byte[24]; // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each System.out.println("allocated 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 80,000,000 bytes"); } }

alt.title: TlabDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var tlabSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 2,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.lines(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), "workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt", "allocate") .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } return } repeat(2_000_000) { tlabSink = ByteArray(24) } // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each println("allocated 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 80,000,000 bytes") }

try.expect: Something like GC(1) TLAB totals: thrds: 1 refills: 300 ... slow allocs: 0 ... waste: 0.3%, followed by Pause Young ... 61M->1M. One thread allocated about 60 MB with about 300 refills, so roughly 5,000 arrays took the fast path for every trip to the shared eden. slow allocs: 0 means no array had to bypass its TLAB. The exact counts change from run to run.

sections.h: Count bytes with the thread's allocation counter
sections.html:
HotSpot counts every byte each thread allocates. com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean, an extension of the standard ThreadMXBean, gives you the counter with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() (since JDK 14):

Java
var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
byte[] receipt = new byte[1 << 20];
long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;   // 1,048,592
Kotlin
val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean
val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes
val receipt = ByteArray(1 shl 20)
val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before          // 1,048,592

The Javadoc calls the number "an approximation". For code that runs once, it is exact to the byte in practice: 1 MiB of data plus a 16-byte array header gave 1,048,592 in 20 out of 20 runs on JDK 21. That makes it the best tool to test your model from lesson 1. A thousand uncached Long boxes allocate 24,000 bytes, exactly 1,000 times 24.

There are two traps.

The first call to anything pays for one-time setup. The first Long.valueOf builds the JDK's cache of the 256 boxes from -128 to 127, and that cost 7,440 bytes in the demo. The first string concatenation bootstraps itself and cost about 137 KB. Measure twice and trust the second number.

The counter returns -1 on a virtual thread. If your Quarkus endpoint runs with @RunOnVirtualThread, measure its code in a test on a platform thread.

In a test, the pattern is: call the code once on tiny input so its classes are loaded, measure one call on real input, and compare the bytes with what the result itself needs, plus a margin. A method that returns a long[500] needs 4,016 bytes. If it allocates 1.5 MB, something inside it is boxing. That comparison is deterministic, and it is exactly what the lab's tests do.

The counter is for questions like "which step of this request allocates?" For the allocation rate of a whole running service, use JFR or the GC log. The performance track covers JFR, and lesson 6 of this track reads GC logs.

try.title: Predict four allocation counts
steps: Read AllocationCounterDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Write down your prediction for each line, for the first run and the second.
Run it with the command below.
Explain each difference between the first and the second column.

code.title: AllocationCounterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ public class AllocationCounterDemo { static final ThreadMXBean THREADS = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static volatile Object sink; // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away static long bytes(Runnable work) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); work.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; } static void show(String what, Runnable work) { long first = bytes(work); // the first run also pays for one-time setup long second = bytes(work); System.out.printf("%-34s %,10d %,11d%n", what, first, second); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("%-34s %10s %11s%n", "bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run"); show("new byte[1 MiB]", () -> sink = new byte[1 << 20]); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(i % 128)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(i % 128); }); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(1_000 + i)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(1_000 + i); }); show("1,000 x \"pay-\" + i", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = "pay-" + i; }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("on a virtual thread the counter says " + THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes())).join(); } }

alt.title: AllocationCounterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean @Volatile private var sink: Any? = null // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away private fun bytes(work: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes work() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before } private fun show(what: String, work: () -> Unit) { val first = bytes(work) // the first run also pays for one-time setup val second = bytes(work) println("%-34s %,10d %,11d".format(what, first, second)) } /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ fun main() { println("%-34s %10s %11s".format("bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run")) show("ByteArray(1 MiB)") { sink = ByteArray(1 shl 20) } show("1,000 x boxing (i % 128).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (i % 128).toLong() } show("1,000 x boxing (1_000 + i).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (1_000 + i).toLong() } show("1,000 x \"pay-\$i\"") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = "pay-$i" } Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("on a virtual thread the counter says ${THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes}") }.join() }

try.expect: The 1 MiB array costs 1,048,592 bytes both times. Long.valueOf(i % 128) costs 7,440 bytes the first time (building the box cache) and 0 after, because every value comes from the cache. Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) costs 24,000 both times. String concatenation costs about 184,000 bytes the first time and about 48,000 after: 48 bytes per id. On the virtual thread the counter says -1.

sections.h: Escape analysis can delete an allocation
sections.html:
Sometimes new allocates nothing. C2, the JIT compiler that optimizes hot methods, runs escape analysis: after inlining (copying small methods into the method that calls them), it checks whether an object can be seen outside the method it is compiling. If it can't, C2 can skip the object and keep its fields in registers. That step is called scalar replacement.

Java
record Point(long x, long y) {}

static long sumPoints(int n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        Point p = new Point(i, i + 1);   // p never leaves the method
        s += p.x() + p.y();
    }
    return s;
}
Kotlin
data class Point(val x: Long, val y: Long)

fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long {
    var s = 0L
    for (i in 0 until n) {
        val p = Point(i.toLong(), i + 1L)   // p never leaves the function
        s += p.x + p.y
    }
    return s
}

Call it ten times with n = 1,000,000 and count the bytes of each call. On JDK 21, the first rounds allocated a few megabytes (3 MB, then 19 MB in one run; the numbers change every run), and from round 4 or so, each round allocated 0 bytes. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes: a million 32-byte points.

Look at the first rounds again. The interpreter and C1, the quick JIT compiler, allocate every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 has compiled the method, and when that happens depends on timing. So never assert "allocates nothing" in a unit test. It can pass on your laptop and fail in CI. The lab asserts only the allocations the code really needs.

An object escapes when you store it in a field, an array or a collection, return it, or pass it to a method that C2 doesn't inline. C2 also won't scalar-replace an array with more than 64 elements (the EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit flag). Escape analysis is a bonus you get in tight loops. It won't save a design that puts every amount into a HashMap<Integer, Long>, because the boxes live on inside the map.

try.title: Watch an allocation disappear, then bring it back
steps: Run EscapeDemo. It runs the measurement in two child JVMs: one with default flags, one with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis.

Now make p escape. In the Java version add static Point last; to the class and last = p; inside the loop. In Kotlin add a top-level var last: KPoint? = null and last = p. Predict the new numbers, then run it again.
Remove the change when you are done.

code.title: EscapeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** * Sums a million short-lived Points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ public class EscapeDemo { record Point(long x, long y) {} // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves this method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags: escape analysis on"); Jvm.run(List.of(), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); System.out.println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"); Jvm.run(List.of("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); return; } ThreadMXBean threads = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long checksum = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 10; round++) { long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000); long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; System.out.printf("round %d: %,12d bytes%n", round, bytes); } System.out.println("checksum " + checksum); } }

alt.title: EscapeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory data class KPoint(val x: Long, val y: Long) // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = KPoint(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves this function s += p.x + p.y } return s } /** * Sums a million short-lived points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags: escape analysis on") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis") Jvm.run(listOf("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") return } val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean var checksum = 0L for (round in 0 until 10) { val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before println("round %d: %,12d bytes".format(round, bytes)) } println("checksum $checksum") }

try.expect: With default flags, the first few rounds allocate megabytes and then the count drops to 0 and stays there. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocates 32,000,000 bytes. After you add last = p, the default run also allocates 32,000,000 bytes in every round, because the point now escapes into a static field and C2 has to create it.

sections.html:
Most of the allocation in a service doesn't come from your own new statements. It hides in boxing, in collection helpers and in string building. The lab's settlement batch is a typical case:

Java
Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < merchantIds.length; i++) {
    totals.merge(merchantIds[i], amountsMinor[i], Long::sum);   // boxes the key, the amount and the sum
}
Kotlin
val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>()
for (i in merchantIds.indices) {
    totals.merge(merchantIds[i], amountsMinor[i]) { a, b -> a + b }   // the same three boxes
}

For 20,000 payments over 500 merchants this allocates 1,539,040 bytes, about 77 bytes per payment. Merchant ids above 127 become new Integer boxes, and every amount and every running sum becomes a new 24-byte Long. The caller only needs one total per merchant: a long[500] of 4,016 bytes. Index the array by merchant id and you get the same answer with no garbage.

These are the usual suspects in payment code:

  • Boxed collections: List<Long>, Map<String, Integer>, and in Kotlin anything typed Long? or used as a type argument.
  • Helpers that copy: toList(), map {}, windowed, zip, and streams of boxed values.
  • Strings: each "pay-" + i costs 48 bytes (a String and its array), and String.format also allocates a varargs array and boxes its arguments.
  • BigDecimal arithmetic: a fee computed as amount.multiply(rate).setScale(2, HALF_EVEN) allocated 184 bytes per call in my measurement, even after warm-up.
  • Lambdas that capture local variables, which create a new object each time the expression runs.

Don't chase every allocation. A request that allocates 50 KB is fine. Fix the loops over large batches, and the code a profile shows behind a young GC that runs several times a second. Measure, change one thing, and measure again.

A check before the lab: amounts.map { it * 2 }.sum() in Kotlin, or amounts.stream().map(a -> a * 2).toList() in Java, on a list of 10,000 amounts above 1,000 cents. Count the objects each one creates and estimate the bytes. (About 10,000 new 24-byte Long boxes and a 40 KB array for the new list, so roughly 280 KB. Summing over a LongArray creates nothing.)

analogy: A TLAB is a cashier's own cash drawer. Taking change from your own drawer needs no one's permission, so it's fast. When the drawer runs low, you walk to the vault and sign for a new bundle of notes: that's the slow path, and it's rare. A humongous object is a pallet that never goes in a drawer and goes straight to the warehouse floor. The analogy breaks at the end of the day: a cashier counts the money out, but the garbage collector never looks at the dead objects in a TLAB. It copies the few live ones and reuses the whole drawer.
world: A settlement job that computes interchange fees with BigDecimal for 10 million card transactions allocates about 1.8 GB for the arithmetic alone, at 184 bytes per fee. The same fee in long minor units with basis points allocates nothing, and the worked example shows how to keep the exact rounding rule. In a Kafka consumer, look at the per-record path: the deserialized DTO, every boxed Long id, every log line built with String.format. When the young GC runs several times a second on a quiet topic, that path is where the bytes come from. And if the code runs under Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, measure it in a test on a platform thread, because the counter says -1 on a virtual one.
mistake: Pooling short-lived objects to "save allocation". It sounds thrifty, but for the collector it's the expensive choice. A temporary object that dies in eden costs almost nothing, because a young collection copies only survivors. A pooled object survives, so the collector copies it to survivor space and then to the old generation, and every young object you store into it later must be tracked by the write barrier (lesson 4). Pools also need locking and reset logic, and a missed reset leaks one request's data into the next. Allocate short-lived objects freely, remove boxing from big loops, and keep pools for things that are truly expensive to create: connections, threads and large direct buffers.

compare.title: A money type with and without an object

java.title: Cents.java
java.html: // Java: a record is always an object (escape analysis may remove short-lived ones) record Cents(long value) { Cents plus(Cents other) { return new Cents(value + other.value); } // a new 24-byte object } Cents total = new Cents(0); for (long a : amountsMinor) total = total.plus(new Cents(a));

kotlin.title: Cents.kt
kotlin.html: // Kotlin: a value class is a plain long at runtime, unless it has to be boxed @JvmInline value class Cents(val value: Long) { operator fun plus(other: Cents) = Cents(value + other.value) // compiles to long + long } var total = Cents(0) for (a in amountsMinor) total += Cents(a) // no objects

compare.note: The Kotlin value class compiles to a raw long in fields, parameters and return types, so the loop allocates nothing even in the interpreter. The Java record is a real object each time; C2 may scalar-replace the short-lived ones in a hot loop, but you can't count on it. The Kotlin version boxes as soon as the value is used as a type argument, a nullable type or Any: a List<Cents> or a Cents? holds boxed objects again, just like List<Long> does.

worked.title: Take the allocation out of a fee calculation

steps.say: A card fee is 1.75% of the amount, rounded half-even to the cent. The settlement job calls this 10 million times a night. Measure it first: with the allocation counter around 10,000 calls, it allocates 1,840,000 bytes, 184 per call, and the number stays the same after warm-up.
steps.code: static final BigDecimal RATE = new BigDecimal("0.0175"); static long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { BigDecimal amount = BigDecimal.valueOf(amountMinor, 2); // a new BigDecimal BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(RATE).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // two more return fee.unscaledValue().longValueExact(); // and a BigInteger }

alt.html: val RATE = BigDecimal("0.0175") fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long { val amount = BigDecimal.valueOf(amountMinor, 2) // a new BigDecimal val fee = (amount * RATE).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) // two more return fee.unscaledValue().longValueExact() // and a BigInteger }

steps.say: Do the same arithmetic in long. 1.75% is 175 basis points, so the exact fee in cents is amountMinor * 175 / 10_000. Integer division drops the remainder, so the rounding rule has to be written out: round up above half, and on exactly half, round to the even neighbour. This version is for amounts of zero or more; refunds go in as positive amounts.
steps.code: static long feeMinor(long amountMinor, int basisPoints) { // 1. scale: cents x basis points, exact in a long for any real payment long scaled = amountMinor * basisPoints; // 2. divide, keeping the remainder long fee = scaled / 10_000, rest = scaled % 10_000; // 3. round half-even, the same rule as RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN if (rest > 5_000 || (rest == 5_000 && fee % 2 == 1)) fee++; return fee; }

alt.html: fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long, basisPoints: Int): Long { // 1. scale: cents x basis points, exact in a long for any real payment val scaled = amountMinor * basisPoints // 2. divide, keeping the remainder var fee = scaled / 10_000 val rest = scaled % 10_000 // 3. round half-even, the same rule as RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN if (rest > 5_000 || (rest == 5_000L && fee % 2 == 1L)) fee++ return fee }

steps.say: Prove the two agree before you switch. Compare them on every amount from 0 to 1,999,999 cents, which includes every exact-half case at this rate. The run behind this lesson found 0 mismatches. Then measure again: the long version allocated 0 bytes for 10,000 calls, in the interpreter and after warm-up.
steps.code: for (long amount = 0; amount < 2_000_000; amount++) { if (feeMinorBig(amount) != feeMinor(amount, 175)) throw new AssertionError("differs at " + amount); }

alt.html: for (amount in 0L until 2_000_000L) { check(feeMinorBig(amount) == feeMinor(amount, 175)) { "differs at $amount" } }

lab.title: Make a settlement batch allocate only its result
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. The two that pass check the answers: the batch code is correct, only wasteful. Read the failure messages: totalsByMerchant allocates about 1.5 MB where its result is 4,016 bytes.
Write AllocationMeter.bytesAllocatedBy: read the counter, run the block, read it again. Throw IllegalStateException if the counter is -1, which is what a virtual thread gets.
Rewrite totalsByMerchant with one LongArray(merchantCount) indexed by merchant id.
Rewrite rollingSums with a running sum: add the first window amounts, then for each step add the amount that enters the window and subtract the one that leaves.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: for (i in merchantIds.indices) compiles to a plain index loop over the array. It allocates no iterator and no range object.
The tests call each method once on tiny input before they measure. That loads every class the method uses, so one-time setup doesn't count against you.
The allocation tests allow 512 bytes above the result array. Any boxing at all blows through that: 20,000 boxes are 480,000 bytes.

drill.title: Write the allocation meter from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write a function that returns the number of bytes a block of code allocates on the current thread. Make it refuse to run where the counter doesn't work. Which threads are those?

answer.html: static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean THREADS = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static long bytesAllocatedBy(Runnable block) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); if (before < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("no counter here: use a platform thread"); // -1 on a virtual thread block.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; }

alt.html: private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean fun bytesAllocatedBy(block: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes check(before >= 0) { "no counter here: use a platform thread" } // -1 on a virtual thread block() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before }

recap: Each thread allocates inside its own TLAB, a chunk of eden, by bumping a pointer. Only a refill touches shared memory, and G1's humongous objects skip TLABs entirely.
new is cheap. The allocation rate is what costs you, because it decides how often eden fills and the young GC runs.
com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() counts a thread's bytes exactly. Measure twice to skip one-time setup, and never on a virtual thread, where it returns -1.
C2's escape analysis can remove an object that never leaves a compiled method. It only happens after C2 compiles the code, so show it in demos and never assert it in tests.
Most allocation hides in boxing, copying helpers, strings and BigDecimal. Use primitive arrays in big loops, and measure before and after each change.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Allocation is free on the JVM, so I never think about it." Explain in your own words what is true in that, and what is missing.
explain.answer: The allocation itself is nearly free. Each thread owns a TLAB in eden and allocates by bumping a pointer, with no locking, and dead young objects cost the collector almost nothing because it only copies survivors. What's missing is the rate. Every byte allocated brings the next young GC closer, so a hot path that boxes every amount or builds strings per record makes the collector pause more often. Escape analysis can remove some short-lived objects, but only after C2 compiles the code and only if they never escape. So: don't fear new, but measure the bytes in big loops and per-record paths, and remove boxing there.

deeper.html:
The TLAB trace line has more in it than the debug summary. With -Xlog:gc+tlab=trace, each refill prints a line like this one from JDK 21:

TLAB: fill thread: 0x00007f79d401a8a0 [id: 22952] desired_size: 266KB slow allocs: 0  refill waste: 4256B alloc: 0.99998     1024KB refills: 1 waste  0.0% gc: 0B slow: 0B

desired_size is the TLAB size the JVM is aiming for this thread. It adapts to how fast the thread allocates and how many threads share eden. refill waste is the most free space the JVM is willing to throw away to start a new TLAB. When an object doesn't fit and less than that is left, the thread abandons the rest of its TLAB and takes a new one. When more is left, the thread keeps its TLAB, allocates that one object directly in eden, and counts a slow alloc. The abandoned tail of a TLAB is filled with a dummy object so the heap stays walkable, and the waste percentage counts those tails.

Escape analysis helps with locks too. If an object never escapes, no other thread can ever lock it, so C2 can drop the synchronized blocks on it. A local StringBuffer, whose methods are all synchronized, is the classic example.

Finally, the counter you used is per thread. getThreadAllocatedBytes(long[] ids) reads it for other threads too. For a whole service, JFR records allocation events at TLAB refills and at allocations outside a TLAB, with stack traces, so it can show which code allocates the most. The per-second rate from JFR or the GC log tells you whether allocation is a problem at all; the per-block counter then tells you where the bytes come from.
